column2: Why promote one artifact from test to production rather than rebuild it?
column3: Production receives the tested bytes; rebuilding can introduce different dependencies or build inputs.

column2: Does replacing the bytes behind an existing release version preserve artifact immutability?
column3: No. Publish a new version or digest instead of changing the content identified by the old release.

column2: Why identify a promoted artifact by digest as well as a friendly version?
column3: The digest identifies content and helps detect substitution; a mutable name alone does not.

column2: Name three uncontrolled inputs that can break reproducible builds.
column3: Unpinned dependencies, embedded timestamps and environment-dependent paths or locale settings.

column2: What does a reproducible build allow an independent builder to demonstrate?
column3: The same source, defined environment and instructions reproduce bit-for-bit identical specified artifacts.

column2: Which is idempotent: ensuring a group exists, or creating a new uniquely named group on every run?
column3: Ensuring the group exists. Repeating it preserves the intended final state.

column2: How does immutable infrastructure handle a configuration change?
column3: Create a replacement from the desired configuration and replace the old instance, rather than accumulating in-place edits.

column2: How can build and release authority be separated?
column3: Let CI publish validated artifacts while a separately authorised deployment identity promotes approved artifacts to production.

column2: Why run a fast syntax check before an expensive integration suite?
column3: It exposes a decisive, inexpensive failure early and avoids wasting execution time.

column2: A deployment corrupts data using an irreversible migration. Is restoring the old binary sufficient?
column3: No. Recovery needs a compatible data-restoration plan or a forward fix; binary rollback alone cannot reverse data changes.

column2: What is the main governance trade-off between centralised and decentralised CI/CD ownership?
column3: Centralisation simplifies consistent controls but can bottleneck teams; decentralisation increases autonomy but needs mechanisms to prevent divergence.

column2: How can a monorepo simplify a change spanning several components?
column3: It permits one coordinated change across components, while requiring dependency-aware validation and appropriate access boundaries.

column2: What delivery challenge grows when tightly coupled components live in separate repositories?
column3: Coordinating compatible versions and cross-repository changes without one atomic commit.

column2: When are separate build and deployment pipelines useful?
column3: When deployments need an independent schedule, identity or approval boundary and consume an explicitly identified validated artifact.

column2: Which delivery decisions should an enterprise usually standardise centrally?
column3: Required security and audit outcomes; teams can choose implementation details within those constraints.

column2: When might self-hosted execution be necessary?
column3: When a job needs private connectivity, specialised hardware or configuration unavailable in an approved hosted option.

column2: What operational responsibilities accompany self-hosted agents?
column3: Provisioning, patching, isolation, capacity, credentials and reliable cleanup of the execution environment.

column2: Where is the key trust boundary when a pull request proposes a deployment script change?
column3: Untrusted source content would gain execution authority, potentially including deployment credentials and production access.

column2: What makes one shared runner pool a potential scaling bottleneck?
column3: Competing workloads queue for finite capacity, and shared failures or maintenance can affect many pipelines.

column2: Why version shared pipeline components before broad adoption?
column3: Consumers can use a known revision and adopt tested updates deliberately, reducing fleet-wide breakage.
